description: Writing if-elif-else, for and while loops in Python, including nested structures.
content_html:
The Three Programming Constructs

Every program, regardless of language, is built from three fundamental constructs: sequence, selection, and iteration. Python implements all three. Any problem that can be solved by a computer can be solved using these three constructs alone — a theorem first proved in the 1960s and still the foundation of every language written since.

Selection — if, elif, else

Selection lets a program make decisions. Python uses if, elif (else if), and else to branch between different blocks of code depending on conditions. Only the block whose condition is True executes; all others are skipped.

# Classify an exam score
score = int(input("Enter score: "))

if score >= 70:
    print("Distinction")
elif score >= 50:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")

Python checks conditions from top to bottom and executes the first block whose condition is True. Once a match is found, the remaining branches are skipped. If no condition is true, the else block (if present) executes.

Key Fact

Python uses indentation (four spaces) to define code blocks — there are no ENDIF or END keywords. Each if, elif, and else line ends with a colon. Forgetting the colon or getting the indentation wrong causes a syntax error.

Count-Controlled Iteration — for with range()

Definite iteration uses a for loop with range(). You know in advance how many times the loop will run. The loop variable takes each value in the sequence, one at a time.

# Print the 3 times table from 1 to 10
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(i, "x 3 =", i * 3)

range(1, 11) produces the integers 1, 2, 3…10. The end value (11) is excluded — this is one of the most common mistakes students make. range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (starting from 0). range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

A running total (accumulator) is a variable that collects a sum inside a loop. Predict the output first, then trace through:

total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total = total + i
print(total)

Trace: i=1 → total=1; i=2 → total=3; i=3 → total=6; i=4 → total=10. Output: 10. The loop adds 1+2+3+4 = 10. Notice that total must be initialised to 0 before the loop begins — otherwise Python raises a NameError.

Iterating Over a Collection

A for loop can also iterate directly over the items in a list or the characters in a string, without needing range():

grades = ["Pass", "Fail", "Pass", "Distinction"]
for grade in grades:
    print(grade)

Each time the loop runs, grade takes the next value from the list. When all items have been processed, the loop ends automatically. This pattern is used constantly when working with lists of student records, sensor readings, or transaction histories.

Condition-Controlled Iteration — while

Indefinite iteration uses a while loop. The condition is tested before each pass. If the condition is False on first entry, the body never runs.

# Keep asking until a valid score is entered
score = -1
while score < 0 or score > 100:
    score = int(input("Enter a score between 0 and 100: "))
print("Valid score:", score)

The number of iterations is not fixed — it depends entirely on what the user enters. This is indefinite iteration. A while loop is the right choice when you cannot know in advance how many passes will be needed.

Key Fact

An infinite loop occurs when the while condition never becomes False. This usually happens because the variable in the condition is never updated inside the loop body. Always check that something inside the loop will eventually make the condition fail.

Nested Structures

Nesting means placing one construct inside another. Loops can be nested inside loops; if statements can be nested inside loops; and conditions can contain multiple levels of elif. Nested structures are used for processing 2D data, multi-condition menus, and grid operations.

Count how many scores in a list are above 60:

scores = [45, 72, 88, 30, 65]
count = 0
for score in scores:
    if score > 60:
        count = count + 1
print("Scores above 60:", count)

Predict: The loop visits 45 (no), 72 (yes, count=1), 88 (yes, count=2), 30 (no), 65 (yes, count=3). Output: Scores above 60: 3. A common mistake is indenting the print inside the loop, which would print after every iteration instead of once at the end.

Single Entry and Exit Points

Well-structured code has a single entry point and a single exit point for each block. In Python, each loop or selection block has one entry (the first line) and one exit (when the condition fails or the block ends). Avoid designs that “break out” of the middle of multiple nested loops — these make code harder to trace, test and maintain.

Use for when: you know the number of iterations in advance, or you are processing every item in a list or string. Examples: printing a times table up to 12, processing each student's score in a class list.

Use while when: the number of iterations depends on user input or a changing condition. Examples: a login prompt that repeats until the correct password is entered, a sensor loop that runs until a threshold is crossed.
exam_tip_html: For “Complete an Algorithm” questions, read the existing code carefully before writing anything — this is the “Investigate” step in the PRIMM approach. Check: does the loop need range() or direct iteration over a list? Is there an accumulator variable that needs initialising? For “Write a Subprogram” questions, identify inputs first, then write the loop or selection logic, then write the output or return value. A common error is placing the print inside the loop when it should be outside.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Python uses if/elif/else for selection. Conditions are tested top to bottom; the first True branch runs and the rest are skipped.
  • Use for with range() for count-controlled loops and for item in collection to iterate over a list or string. Use while when the number of repetitions is not known in advance.
  • An infinite loop happens when the while condition never becomes False. Always ensure the loop body can change the condition variable.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a for loop and a while loop in Python.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A for loop is count-controlled and runs a fixed number of times known in advance (1); a while loop is condition-controlled and runs while a condition is True, so the number of iterations is not fixed (1).
Secure: Both loops mentioned but the distinction is imprecise.
Developing: One loop described correctly without comparison.
Emerging: Both described as identical or neither correct.

practice_questions.text: Write Python code for a program that asks the user to enter a number between 1 and 10. The program should keep asking until a valid number is entered, then print the number.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Variable initialised outside loop (1); while loop with correct condition e.g. num < 1 or num > 10 (1); input() with int() conversion inside loop (1); loop repeats correctly until valid input (1); print() after loop exits (1); meaningful identifier name (1).
Secure: Loop structure correct; minor error in condition or conversion.
Developing: Loop present but condition or conversion wrong.
Emerging: No loop — sequential structure only.

Mastering: i=1 count=0 (odd); i=2 count=1 (even); i=3 count=1; i=4 count=2; i=5 count=2; output 2. Mark per correct iteration row (4 marks for correctly identifying the two even numbers and final count).
Secure: Three iterations correct with correct final output.
Developing: Two iterations correct.
Emerging: Does not understand the modulus condition.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the following Python code will result in an infinite loop, and write a corrected version.
password = ""
while password != "secret":
    print("Access denied")
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The variable password is never updated inside the loop (1) so the condition password != 'secret' is always True (1); corrected version includes password = input() inside the loop (1); explanation that updating the variable allows the condition to eventually become False (1).
Secure: Infinite loop identified with partial correction.
Developing: Identifies a problem but does not explain why it loops forever.
Emerging: No understanding of why the loop continues.

Mastering: The program prints every integer from 1 to 10 (1) that is divisible by 3, i.e. 3, 6, 9 (1).
Secure: Correct in meaning with one detail missing.
Developing: Identifies it loops from 1 to 10 but misunderstands the condition.
Emerging: Describes what each line does individually rather than the overall purpose.

practice_questions.text: A programmer wants to write a program that reads exam scores for a class of 30 students and counts how many scored above 75. Discuss whether a for loop or a while loop is more appropriate for this task, and write the Python code.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For loop identified as more appropriate (1); reason — 30 iterations known in advance (1); counter variable initialised to 0 (1); for loop with range(30) or equivalent (1); if score > 75 inside loop increments counter (1); print result after loop (1).
Secure: Correct loop type with working code minus one element.
Developing: Correct reasoning without complete code.
Emerging: Wrong loop choice or no working code.

knowledge_checks.q: Which Python statement would loop from 1 to 5 inclusive (i.e. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)?
A while loop checks its condition _____.
A for loop is an example of _____ iteration because the number of repetitions is fixed in advance.
Placing one loop or selection construct inside another is called _____.
Match each construct to its Python keyword.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of iteration does a while loop implement?
What type of iteration does a for loop with range() implement?
A while loop checks its condition _____ the body runs.
flashcard_questions.a: Before — the body may never execute if the condition is False from the start.

flashcard_questions.q: What causes an infinite loop in a while construct?
flashcard_questions.a: The condition variable is never updated inside the loop body.

flashcard_questions.q: In Python, what marks the start of a code block inside an if or loop?
flashcard_questions.a: A colon at the end of the header line and consistent indentation.

flashcard_questions.q: How do you iterate over every item in a list called scores without using range()?
flashcard_questions.a: for score in scores: — the loop variable takes each value in turn.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the term for placing one loop inside another?
An accumulator pattern requires initialising a variable to _____ before the loop.
How many branches can an if/elif/else chain have?
flashcard_questions.a: Any number — one if, zero or more elif, and an optional else at the end.

glossary_terms.definition: The programming construct in which instructions are executed one after another in the order they appear in the code.
The programming construct in which the program chooses between different execution paths based on a condition.
The programming construct in which a block of instructions repeats, either a set number of times or while a condition holds.
A count-controlled loop that iterates a fixed number of times, with Python's range() function supplying the sequence of values.
A condition-controlled loop that checks its condition before each iteration; if the condition is False from the start, the body never executes.
A programming structure where one loop or selection construct is placed inside another, creating multiple levels of control flow.
